title: How the Internet Works: From Your Device to the World

scenes.heading: A message begins with a question
scenes.caption: Your device asks for information
scenes.takeaway: Every web visit starts with a request
scenes.narration: Open a website on your phone. You tap its name, and a page appears. Behind that simple moment, your device starts a journey: it finds the website, contacts a server, requests information, and brings the answer back.
scenes.visual_title: Tap a name. Start a journey.

scenes.heading: Your device joins a network
scenes.caption: Wi-Fi or mobile data connects you
scenes.takeaway: A local connection is your first step
scenes.narration: First, your device connects to a nearby network. At home, that is usually Wi-Fi through a router. Outside, it may be a mobile network. This connection gives your device a path beyond your room or the cell tower nearby.

scenes.heading: The router is a traffic guide
scenes.caption: Packets need a next direction
scenes.takeaway: Routers forward data toward its destination
scenes.narration: Your router forwards traffic between local devices and the wider internet. It checks where data should go next and sends it onward. It does not need to understand the message itself; it needs enough addressing information to choose a next hop.

scenes.heading: Names are easier than numbers
scenes.caption: People remember names, networks use addresses
scenes.takeaway: A domain name must be resolved to an IP address
scenes.narration: People remember names like example dot com. Networks use numerical Internet Protocol addresses. The Domain Name System, or DNS, connects these two worlds. It helps your device discover the address associated with the name you entered.

scenes.heading: DNS looks up the destination
scenes.caption: A resolver searches for the answer
scenes.takeaway: DNS answers are often cached to save time
scenes.narration: Your device may already have a recent DNS answer stored. Otherwise, it asks a DNS resolver, often provided by your internet service. The resolver finds the requested record and can temporarily cache it, making the next lookup faster.

scenes.heading: The request is divided into packets
scenes.caption: Large data travels in manageable pieces
scenes.takeaway: Packets carry data plus delivery information
scenes.narration: Your device prepares the request for transport. Data travels in packets, small units carrying information needed for delivery. Packets let many conversations share network links, and the receiving system can reassemble the pieces in the right order.

scenes.heading: IP addresses help packets travel
scenes.caption: Addresses identify source and destination
scenes.takeaway: IP provides addressing across interconnected networks
scenes.narration: Internet Protocol gives packets source and destination addresses. These are delivery details, not a complete route map. Network devices examine the destination and decide where to forward each packet, allowing separate networks to communicate.

scenes.heading: Routers pass traffic between networks
scenes.caption: Each hop moves a packet closer
scenes.takeaway: The path can change as network conditions change
scenes.narration: A packet may cross several routers before reaching a server. Each router forwards it toward another network. The path can change as operators adjust routes or avoid unavailable and congested links. The internet is designed to work across many possible paths.

scenes.heading: TCP helps reliable conversations
scenes.caption: The sender and receiver coordinate
scenes.takeaway: TCP can detect loss and retransmit missing data
scenes.narration: Many web connections use Transmission Control Protocol, or TCP, for reliable ordered delivery. The endpoints track the data being exchanged. If information goes missing, TCP can arrange to send it again, helping applications receive a complete stream.

scenes.heading: HTTPS protects the exchange
scenes.caption: Encryption helps keep data private
scenes.takeaway: TLS protects data in transit and authenticates the server
scenes.narration: Websites commonly use HTTPS, which combines HTTP with encryption from TLS. Your browser checks the website certificate and negotiates secure keys. Encryption makes intercepted traffic difficult to read, while authentication helps verify the server you intended to reach.

scenes.heading: The server receives the request
scenes.caption: A data center runs the website
scenes.takeaway: A server is a computer prepared to answer requests
scenes.narration: The packets reach a web server: a computer running software that listens for requests and sends responses. Large websites may use many servers in different data centers. They share work, store content, and help keep services available.

scenes.heading: The application builds a response
scenes.caption: Code and data become a web page
scenes.takeaway: The response may combine templates, data, and media
scenes.narration: The server application decides what to send. It may read a database, run code, choose a page template, and prepare images or other files. Some pages are ready to send; others are assembled for your particular request.

scenes.heading: The response travels home
scenes.caption: Packets return across the network
scenes.takeaway: The reply follows network routes back to your device
scenes.narration: The response travels back through routers and network links. Packets may take different paths on the way home. Your device receives them, while transport protocols handle ordering and missing data. The browser can begin processing before every file arrives.

scenes.heading: Your browser turns data into a page
scenes.caption: HTML, CSS, and JavaScript shape the result
scenes.takeaway: The browser parses, lays out, and paints content
scenes.narration: Your browser interprets the response. HTML describes structure, CSS controls appearance, and JavaScript adds interactive behavior. The browser calculates layout, paints pixels, and updates the screen as resources arrive. Text may appear while images continue loading.

scenes.heading: Caching avoids repeated journeys
scenes.caption: Nearby copies can make loading faster
scenes.takeaway: Caches reduce delay and network traffic
scenes.narration: Your browser may reuse cached images, scripts, and stylesheets instead of downloading them again. Content delivery networks also keep copies closer to viewers. Valid cached files reduce waiting time and the amount of data crossing long distances.

scenes.heading: Many systems cooperate
scenes.caption: No single machine is the internet
scenes.takeaway: The internet is a network of networks
scenes.narration: A website visit depends on your device, router, provider, DNS, transit networks, data centers, servers, and browser software. No single organization owns the whole internet. Shared standards let equipment and services around the world communicate.

scenes.heading: The whole journey happens quickly
scenes.caption: A few seconds hide many coordinated steps
scenes.takeaway: Name lookup, routing, secure transport, and rendering work together
scenes.narration: Next time a website appears after one tap, remember the hidden journey. Your device connects, DNS finds an address, packets cross networks, secure protocols protect the exchange, a server responds, and your browser renders the page.
